word:greek-nt:G0034.explanation: Agelē means a herd of animals.

word:greek-nt:G0041.explanation: Hagiotēs means holiness or sanctity, an abstract quality.

word:greek-nt:G0117.explanation: Athēnaios means Athenian, describing someone belonging to Athens.

word:greek-nt:G0148.explanation: Aischrologia means filthy speech or foul language.

word:greek-nt:G0306.explanation: The word means “to adjourn a proceeding” or “to defer,” describing the decision to postpone a formal hearing or matter rather than continue it immediately. It functions as an action word: someone delays the proceeding until a later time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 24:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is postponement of an official proceeding.

word:greek-nt:G0399.explanation: Anaphero means to carry or lead something up, and it can also mean to offer up a sacrifice.

word:greek-nt:G0409.explanation: Androphonos means a murderer or manslayer.

word:greek-nt:G0430.explanation: Anechomai means to endure, bear with, or put up with. It can describe bearing with a faithless and perverse generation.

word:greek-nt:G0496.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to resist” or “resisting”—actively opposing or refusing to yield to someone or something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 7:51, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains direct opposition: standing against what is being said or done rather than accepting or following it.

word:greek-nt:G0618.explanation: Apolambanō means to receive or get back. It can also describe receiving what is due or deserved. In another use, it means to draw aside or separate.

word:greek-nt:G0647.explanation: Apostasion means divorce. It can also refer to a written bill of divorce.

word:greek-nt:G0702.explanation: Haretas is the personal name Aretas, identified as Aretas IV, king of the Nabataeans. Aretas is the king whose governor guarded the city of Damascus.

word:greek-nt:G0795.explanation: Astocheō means to miss the mark or fail. It can also describe people who wander away from the faith.

word:greek-nt:G0935.explanation: Basileus means king or ruler, as when David is called king.

word:greek-nt:G1073.explanation: Gemo means to be full of. It can describe a mouth full of cursing or bowls full of incense.

word:greek-nt:G1110.explanation: Gnostos means known. It can also refer to an acquaintance.

word:greek-nt:G1129.explanation: Gymnasia means physical exercise or training.

word:greek-nt:G1226.explanation: Diabebaioomai means to assert emphatically—to affirm or insist confidently.

word:greek-nt:G1280.explanation: Diaporeō means to be perplexed or in doubt.

word:greek-nt:G1352.explanation: Dio means therefore or wherefore, linking what follows to a preceding reason or circumstance.

word:greek-nt:G1514.explanation: Eirēneuō means to be at peace or to live peaceably with others.

word:greek-nt:G1561.explanation: This word means “expectation”: an anticipated outcome or something looked toward with anticipation. It functions as a noun, naming what is awaited rather than describing an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so this single occurrence represents its known use in that corpus. It appears in Hebrews 10:27, but the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage rather than on the word alone.

word:greek-nt:G1640.explanation: Elassōn means less or inferior. It can also mean younger, contrasting an elder with a younger person.

word:greek-nt:G1679.explanation: Elpizō means to hope for something or to trust in someone.

word:greek-nt:G1705.explanation: Empiplēmi means to fill up or satisfy, as when the hungry are filled with good things.

word:greek-nt:G1792.explanation: Entryphao means to revel or riot.

word:greek-nt:G1846.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to dig out” or “to dig through.” It describes removing earth or breaking through a barrier by digging. The idea is active and practical: someone makes an opening or clears a way by excavation. It occurs two times in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 2:4 and Galatians 4:15. In ordinary reading, its precise force depends on whether the sentence emphasizes creating an opening, removing material, or bringing something out through digging.

word:greek-nt:G2007.explanation: Epitithemi means to put, place, or lay something on something else, including laying hands on a person.

word:greek-nt:G2270.explanation: Hēsychazō means to be quiet or silent. In some contexts, it describes ceasing and living quietly as well.

word:greek-nt:G2403.explanation: Iezabel is a personal name, used for a false prophetess.

word:greek-nt:G2616.explanation: Katadynasteuō means to treat harshly or oppress someone.

word:greek-nt:G2689.explanation: Katastolē means clothing, dress, or attire.

word:greek-nt:G2731.explanation: This word means a dwelling—the place where one lives. It refers to a residence or settled home rather than to a person or an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Mark 5:3, so its normal meaning is represented by this single occurrence. The sense remains straightforward: a dwelling is a place of habitation, where someone lives or stays. The surrounding verse context would determine how that idea functions in the passage.

word:greek-nt:G2744.explanation: Kauchaomai means to boast or glory proudly.

word:greek-nt:G2793.explanation: Kindyneuō means to be in danger or peril.

word:greek-nt:G2850.explanation: “Flattery” refers to pleasing or complimentary speech used to gain favor, rather than simply expressing an honest judgment. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 2:5. Its central idea is praise shaped by personal advantage or the desire to influence someone. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular force in that passage.

word:greek-nt:G2869.explanation: Kopazō means to abate, die down, or become still. It is used of wind that ceases.

word:greek-nt:G2928.explanation: Kryptō means to hide or conceal.

word:greek-nt:G3097.explanation: Magos means a sorcerer, magician, or wizard. It can also refer to sages, such as the wise men from the east whom Herod consulted about the appearance of a star.

word:greek-nt:G3163.explanation: Machē means strife, contention, or quarrel.

word:greek-nt:G3332.explanation: Metēren means to depart or move on.

word:greek-nt:G3408.explanation: Misthos means pay or wages. It can also mean a reward.

word:greek-nt:G3457.explanation: This word refers to a millstone, the heavy stone used for grinding grain. It describes a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 17:2, and is rendered “millstone.” The related expression “of a mill” clarifies that the word concerns the stone associated with a mill. Its precise force in Luke 17:2 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G3501.explanation: Neos means young or youthful. It can also mean new or fresh.

word:greek-nt:G3574.explanation: “A night and a day” refers to a complete period that includes both nighttime and daytime. It functions as a time expression rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. The expression appears in 2 Corinthians 11:25, but understanding its specific force there requires the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G3615.explanation: Oikiakos means a member of a household.

word:greek-nt:G3804.explanation: Pathema means suffering or affliction. It can also refer to passions or emotions.

word:greek-nt:G3871.explanation: Parakalyptō means to hide, conceal, or veil.

word:greek-nt:G3956.explanation: Pas means all or every. It refers to all the generations in a stated sequence and, in another context, to every temptation.

word:greek-nt:G4001.explanation: This word means “five hundred,” expressing the specific number 500. It is a numerical term rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing the same basic numerical meaning in both places. Its exact significance in any sentence comes from the quantity being counted in that surrounding passage. The word appears in Luke 7:41 and 1 Corinthians 15:6. word:greek-nt:G4074.explanation: Petros is a Greek personal name, rendered Peter.

word:greek-nt:G4298.explanation: Prokopto means to advance or make progress. It can also describe going further, as empty chatter goes further in ungodliness.

word:greek-nt:G4315.explanation: Prosabbaton means the day before the Sabbath.

word:greek-nt:G4382.explanation: Prosōpolēmpsia means partiality or favoritism. Scripture says there is no partiality with God.

word:greek-nt:G4463.explanation: This word means “to beat with a rod.” It describes physical punishment carried out with a stick or staff, focusing on the act of striking rather than naming the instrument itself. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 16:22 and 2 Corinthians 11:25. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the experience or action of being beaten with a rod.

word:greek-nt:G4632.explanation: Skeuos means a vessel or container. It can also describe someone chosen as an instrument for a task.

word:greek-nt:G4719.explanation: This form means a head of grain.

word:greek-nt:G4720.explanation: Stachys is a personal name, referring to an individual named Stachys. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 16:9. The English Bible renderings preserve it as “Stachys,” indicating that it functions as a name rather than as a descriptive word translated into an ordinary English term. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain Stachys’s specific role in that passage.

word:greek-nt:G4786.explanation: Synkerannymi means to mix with or unite.

word:greek-nt:G4845.explanation: This word describes something reaching fullness or being overwhelmed, with the basic senses “to (ful)fill” and “to be swamped.” It can therefore refer either to something being brought to completion or to circumstances becoming so full that they overwhelm what is present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Luke and Acts. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on whether the surrounding context emphasizes fulfillment or being overwhelmed.

word:greek-nt:G4900.explanation: Synallassō means to urge or compel people to reconcile.

word:greek-nt:G4939.explanation: Syntrophos means someone brought up with another, including a foster brother. It describes Manaen as having been brought up with Herod.

word:greek-nt:G5091.explanation: Timaō means to honor or to value something.

word:greek-nt:G5176.explanation: Trogōn means to eat or partake of a meal.

word:greek-nt:G5235.explanation: Hyperballō means to surpass, excel, exceed, or go beyond.

word:greek-nt:G5459.explanation: Phōsphoros means light-bearing or radiant, and can refer to the morning star.

word:greek-nt:G5460.explanation: Phōteinos means bright. It can also describe something as full of light.

word:greek-nt:G5565.explanation: Chōris means apart from, separately from, or without.

word:greek-nt:G6036.explanation: This word means “to come in” or “to enter,” describing movement into a place or situation. It is an action word, focusing on arrival from outside rather than simply being present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 21:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of coming into or entering something.
